extracted.intended_audience: students and general readers interested in American state government (particularly European readers seeking comparative understanding)
extracted.subtask_description: A scholarly, comparative account of how U.S. state governments operate in practice: their powers, organizational peculiarities, the composition and behaviour of legislatures, and problems (e.g., special legislation, corruption) that affect legislative and executive quality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Factors affecting municipal creditworthiness
rubrics_metrics.description: Why municipal debt and its security differ from State debt — e.g., cities cannot repudiate, while sovereign States can; State constitutions may restrict municipal borrowing; city government conditions (wealth concentration, ignorant voters) affect creditworthiness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains that inadequate restrictions on municipal borrowing and the disposition of city councils (prone to speculation, jobbery, embezzlement) are chief causes of municipal financial weakness; footnote notes some New England places make municipal debt personal debt of inhabitants, which is 'excellent security.'

rubrics_metrics.name: State as intermediary between nation and municipality
rubrics_metrics.description: A State combines some features characteristic of a nation with others belonging to a municipality; it is lower than the nation but greater than a municipality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This conceptual frame informs expectations about what state governments do and how they are organized — their mix of national-style powers (jurisprudence, taxation, supervision of local government) and local-style administration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scale of powers vs quality of personnel and public interest
rubrics_metrics.description: A State may have vast legal powers (law/order, civil/criminal law, taxation) but be staffed and supported by persons of limited distinction and by a declining level of popular interest or reverence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluation should consider both the formal scope of state authority and the actual calibre of officials and civic engagement, since great legal powers may be wielded by mediocre actors.

rubrics_metrics.name: No single 'typical' State — importance of variation
rubrics_metrics.description: State governments share an organic frame but vary endlessly in functional activities according to temper, habits, ideas, education, and traditions of inhabitants.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyses should avoid treating any single State as representative; illustrations from one State may not apply to others and general statements must be qualified by regional differences.

rubrics_metrics.name: States more democratic than the Federal model (appointments/terms/relations)
rubrics_metrics.description: State constitutions tend to be more democratic than the Federal Constitution: different methods of appointing judges, shorter terms for officials and senators, and altered executive-legislative relationships.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This democratic tendency affects the balance of power — e.g., more directly elected executive officials and less unified executive authority compared with the national cabinet model.

rubrics_metrics.name: Executive structure: independent elected officials vs cabinet unity
rubrics_metrics.description: Unlike the unified Federal executive (President with subordinates), many State executives lack a cabinet — chief executive officials are directly elected and independent of the governor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These officers hold office by titles independent of the governor, are not generally subject to his directions, and are often of different parties or elected at different times/terms; this undermines executive harmony and unified policy-making at the State level.

rubrics_metrics.name: Governor's limited functions compared to the President
rubrics_metrics.description: A State governor lacks foreign policy, vast patronage, command of the national armed forces, and services like a postal system; his main substantive powers are a veto, maintaining order in crises, and routine representative duties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assessment of a governor's importance should focus on veto use, crisis initiative, and ability to suggest legislative remedies; the governor often matters most in emergencies or when using the veto effectively to check the legislature.

rubrics_metrics.name: Executive officers' constrained discretion due to legislative micromanagement
rubrics_metrics.description: State executive officers often perform narrowly defined statutory tasks, are checked by other officials, and operate under detailed statutes that limit discretion; legislative committees supervise them closely.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where legislation specifies purposes for every money grant and exercises inquisitorial supervision, executive discretion is 'extinct' and officers act as 'mere hands' of the legislative brain; this reduces executive policy-making capacity but increases legislative control and opportunities for oversight (and also for legislative corruption).

rubrics_metrics.name: Legislative dominance and institutional weaknesses
rubrics_metrics.description: State legislatures are normally the strongest force in the State but often have fewer able/high-minded men, less recognized leadership, greater temptations, and less vigilant public opinion than national legislatures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluation of State governance must consider the strength of the legislature and its internal quality (leadership, member calibre), since a weakly led legislature surrounded by temptations fosters poor outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classification of State legislative business (three classes)
rubrics_metrics.description: State legislation may be classified as (I) ordinary private law (contracts, torts, family law, procedure), (II) administrative law (local government regulation, public works, education, corporation and labour law, taxation, public debt management), and (III) local and special 'private bills' for charters, franchises, and municipal incorporation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bills of the second class are more numerous than the first, while third-class (local/special) bills outnumber the other two combined; this distribution shapes legislative incentives and corruption risk.

rubrics_metrics.name: Special/local 'private bills' as a source of corruption and confusion
rubrics_metrics.description: Local and special legislation (private bills authorizing charters, franchises, etc.) confuses general law and furnishes opportunities for jobs, speculation, injustice to individuals/localities, and bribery.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These bills are condemned as 'one of the scandals of the country' and a 'perennial fountain of corruption.' Reforms (e.g., requiring application of general laws, pre-filing of appropriations, tabulation/commentary, procedural notices) have been adopted in some States to curb their number and abuse.

rubrics_metrics.name: State legislature control over municipal constitutions and management
rubrics_metrics.description: A significant and pernicious form of special legislation is statutory control of city constitutions and management; cities' rapid growth and revenues make them tempting to speculators and a target for legislative manipulation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: State control over municipal affairs can be a major avenue for political enrichment and corruption; granting cities authority to make their own charters is one reform remedy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Selection by party conventions reduces legislative quality
rubrics_metrics.description: The system of selecting candidates by party conventions tends to prevent entrance of good men and favors the bad.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This selection mechanism is cited as a structural cause of low-quality legislative membership and will be discussed further in later chapters (Part III).

rubrics_metrics.name: Residency-based representation narrows candidate pool
rubrics_metrics.description: Habit of choosing only a resident to represent an electoral district narrows the field, excludes competent men from elsewhere, and deters able men from entering State politics (loss of seat cannot be recouped by running elsewhere).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This parochial rule reduces opportunities to recruit high-quality legislators and limits mobility of political careers within the State.

rubrics_metrics.name: Remoteness and character of State capitals discourage good legislators
rubrics_metrics.description: State capitals are often small, socially unattractive towns remote from major population centres, making them inconvenient for businesspeople and lawyers and shielding legislatures from vigilant public opinion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Physical and social remoteness of capitals (e.g., Hartford vs Harrisburg) is cited as a factor in comparative legislative quality; proximity to population and press scrutiny tends to improve legislative standards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nature of legislative business deters ambitious/able men
rubrics_metrics.description: Much State legislative business consists of numerous local or administrative matters that excite little popular interest; the cumulative importance is large but individually bills seem unimportant, deterring leading politicians.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because much work is 'dreary' (gas, railroad bills, local advantages), ambitious or high-calibre men avoid State legislatures; the public often fails to perceive the aggregate significance of such matters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Payment of legislative salaries has limited effect on member quality
rubrics_metrics.description: Paying members may attract poorer men (farmers, needy lawyers) but would not clearly keep out better men; discontinuing salaries is unlikely to improve legislative quality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author doubts salary removal would attract better men and suggests the same drawbacks/attractions would remain; the point is that pay is not the main determinant of quality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legislative support services improve lawmaking quality
rubrics_metrics.description: Providing legal aid for members in drafting bills, supplying information via state libraries, retaining lawyers for drafting, and using skilled administrative departments and commissions improves the quality of legislation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Wisconsin State Library, New York State Library's drafting assistance, commissions to investigate complex questions; such institutional supports counteract some defects of legislatures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regional and socioeconomic factors shape legislative integrity
rubrics_metrics.description: Legislatures in New England (Massachusetts, Connecticut, Vermont) are generally purer and better, North-Western farmer-populated States are honest though sometimes narrow, while States with large cities and immigrant inflows (New York, Pennsylvania, Illinois, etc.) have suffered greater corruption due to unscrupulous party managers and concentrated capital.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluation of a State's legislature should account for population composition (urban vs rural), immigration, presence of strong corporate interests, and local political traditions; the worst corruption occurs where great capital meets weak material.

rubrics_metrics.name: Corporate money and local special bills as principal corrupting forces
rubrics_metrics.description: Large corporations and money-power attack legislatures (especially in great States) by promoting special bills, buying influence, and blackmailing members; even a small minority of corruptible members can enable extensive abuses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The prevalence of special bills and corporate campaigns for local privileges create opportunities for bribery and jobbery; restraining special legislation and increasing transparency are proposed remedies.
